One-sentence reason for being there: An exploration of how sound, technology, and natural forms can come together through reactive visuals.
My role: For the Hanami Tech project, I was mainly responsible for developing the visual side of the work in TouchDesigner. While my partner worked on the audio analysis, I focused on creating the visual system and shaping how the digital effects responded to the music. This included designing the distortion effects, dynamic lines, and dot-based geometries that formed the main visual elements. One of the main parts of my work was developing the blob tracking system, which allowed us to extract real-time X and Y coordinates from the detected blobs when triggered by the snare. I then used this data to control how the visual effects moved and spread across the blooming sakura, creating a direct connection between the music and the visuals. I also worked on combining the generated geometries with the organic sakura elements, making the visuals react dynamically to the rhythm of the music and creating a continuous interaction between the digital effects and the natural forms.
Short description:
Hanami Tech is an audio-reactive composition inspired by the Japanese tradition of hanami -
the act of watching sakura bloom. We explored this idea through a visual composition where
cherry blossoms slowly open and move in response to the beat of the music.
We also compose the music, combining modern techno sounds with natural visuals to create
a fusion between technology and nature.
Concept/Problem:
The system based on audio analysis. The snare signal is the main driver - it controls blob
tracking, and triggers the opening and closing of the sakura visuals.
On the first playback, the audio remains clean and the visuals outside the blobs. On the
second playback, audio distortion appears and affects the visual system, spreading
distortion areas outside the blobs. The speed of all visual effects are also controlled by
music.
The patch also outputs real-time X and Y coordinates of the tracked blobs, which are used
as part of the visual logic.

Short description: An interactive VR experience that invites the user to explore a mysterious botanical garden filled with magical plants, objects, and hidden spaces. As they move through the environment, they can discover different plants and interact with signs that reveal illustrated encyclopaedia entries, introducing their properties and stories through an antique-inspired interface. Entering a mysterious teapot transports the user into a dark, immersive space where they can uncover the mysterious properties of the herbs and the magical gifts they offer. The experience is built around exploration, interaction, and discovery, allowing the world to unfold through the user’s curiosity.

One-sentence reason for being there: My exploration of identity systems and how one visual language adapts across media.
Short description: Jazzavu Fest is a fictional three-day jazz festival set in New Orleans, created around the idea of celebrating jazz in all its forms. The identity captures the warmth, energy, and freedom of live music through a bold combination of expressive typography, playful illustrations, and a vibrant retro-inspired aesthetic. From the main festival poster to tickets, wristbands, and graphic patterns, every element is designed to feel like part of the same experience. The illustrations of the saxophone, trumpet, and double bass bring the music to life, while the typography adds personality and a sense of movement. The result is an identity that feels festive and inviting, while still having a strong and recognizable character. Jazzavu Fest is ultimately about more than an event — it is an invitation to feel the groove, live the jazz, and become part of the atmosphere.
Concept/Problem: The starting point was the challenge of making a jazz festival feel both authentic and visually fresh, without relying on predictable or overly traditional jazz aesthetics. I explored the shapes of musical instruments and transformed them into bold, simplified graphic elements that could communicate the genre instantly while remaining visually playful. The color palette combines deep purple and red with energetic orange and yellow, balanced by a soft cream background; this contrast creates warmth and gives the compositions a distinctly nostalgic character. I also developed the identity so that its elements could be easily adapted across different physical applications, allowing the same idea to work as a large-scale poster, a small ticket, or a wearable festival wristband.

Short description: Stellar Family Portrait is an interactive educational website for children where stars are represented as characters in one cosmic family. Each character’s design reflects real stellar properties such as color, temperature, age, and brightness. By clicking on a star, users can read its personal story, written in simple and engaging language. This approach transforms complex astronomical data into an emotional and accessible experience, helping children understand the life cycle of stars and the structure of our galaxy.
Concept/Problem: The user sees a group of star characters arranged as a “family portrait.” Clicking on a star opens its profile card, where the star introduces itself and explains its properties (color, temperature, brightness, life stage) in simple language. The user understands that stars are not static points of light, but living systems that change over time. They feel curiosity and empathy toward the stars by seeing them as characters with stories.

One-sentence reason for being there: My exploration of how typography and layout can respond to literary content.
Short description: For “Valleys of Shadow,” I developed a comprehensive editorial design project inspired by the melancholy and haunting atmosphere of Edgar Allan Poe’s poetry. I designed a poetry zine featuring structured double-page spreads for works such as “Eldorado,” “To One in Paradise,” and “Annabel Lee,” focusing on precise typography, visual hierarchy, and cohesive composition. The design uses one limited palette: burnt orange linework on warm cream, which echoes vintage engravings and the twilight mood of the verses. A flowing script typeface gives the poem titles and pull-quotes a handwritten, romantic feel, while a clean serif keeps the verses easy to read. The layout changes with each poem to match its content.

One-sentence reason for being there: I decided to include it in my portfolio because I believe that one of the most honest ways to understand a person is to look at how they treat the people they love.
Short description:
For me, creativity has always been one of the ways I express care. When someone is important to me, I want to notice them, remember the little things about them, and sometimes turn those memories into something they can keep.

This magazine was not made for an assignment, a grade, or a brief. I made it simply because she mattered to me — and because I wanted to give her something that could hold a small piece of the life we shared. In that sense, it is probably one of the most personal things I have ever designed.
Concept/Problem: I created this magazine as a birthday gift for my best friend, bringing together photographs, memories, stories and the small, seemingly insignificant moments that make up our friendship.
